title: Keep my Sikhs
hook: sevak sikh hamaare taareeh: carry my servants and Sikhs across (Chaupai)
tomorrow: The one who spreads and gathers

segments.voice: Yesterday, the enemies within and without, and your line, end the enemy within. Did the one you named show up? Today, the prayer turns outward again, to people. Day three hundred seventy-four.

Picture a wide river in flood, the kind people in Punjab knew well, brown and fast and far too deep to wade. On this bank, everyone you love. On the far bank, safety. There's one boat, and one person who knows how to steer it. You don't ask for yourself first. You ask for them. Take my mother. Take my friend. Take the kids. Get them across. That picture of a river and a crossing runs all through Sikh scripture. And in Chaupai, the Guru uses it to pray for his people. Today: keep my Sikhs.
screen: `A RIVER IN FLOOD.` → `ONE BOAT, ONE PERSON TO STEER.` → `GET THEM ACROSS.`

segments.voice: The line is sevak sikh hamaare taareeahi. Sevak: servants, those who serve. Sikh: learners, disciples. Hamaare: mine. Taareeahi: carry them across. Carry my servants and Sikhs across. The verb is from taarna, to ferry over, to bring someone safely to the other shore. In the Guru Granth Sahib, the world is often pictured as a vast, terrifying ocean, and the Guru, or the Name, as the boat that carries people over it. So when the Tenth Guru prays this line, he's doing something tender. He's a Guru, and he is praying for his disciples, asking God to carry them where he can't carry them himself. Look at how the prayer's circle has been widening. First, protect me. Then, may my family live in peace. Then, all my servants and Sikhs. A few lines on, may my hope be fulfilled, and on it goes. That widening is a very Sikh pattern. The Ardas, the prayer that closes Sikh gatherings, does the same thing. It names the Gurus, the martyrs, the community, and then ends by asking for the good of all, everyone, without exception. You met that on day three hundred thirty. Prayer, in this tradition, almost never stays small. Notice one more thing. This is a prayer said by the community itself, every morning and evening. So when a Sikh recites it, they're saying a prayer the Guru prayed for them. Carry them across. It lands in a different way when you know you're one of the them.
screen: `SEVAK SIKH HAMAARE TAAREEAHI.` · `TAARNA: TO FERRY ACROSS.` · `THE CIRCLE WIDENS: ME, FAMILY, SIKHS.` · `A PRAYER THE GURU PRAYED FOR THEM.` · then, large: `CARRY THEM ACROSS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for a friend by name. Sit and breathe slowly. Bring one friend to mind, someone who's in a hard river right now. Illness, grief, a bad job, a lonely stretch. See their face. Say their name, quietly, out loud if you can. If you pray, you can hold that name in Waheguru, or say the line, carry them across. If you don't pray, simply hold them in your attention for a while and wish them safely to the other bank. Then, if it feels right, let the circle widen: one more name, then everyone in a river like theirs. The bell holds the time.
Keep my Sikhs. Sevak sikh hamaare taareeahi: carry my servants and Sikhs across, the Guru praying for his people over the river.
Your line: carry them across. Today, send that friend a short message, no advice, just letting them know they were held in mind this morning. Day three hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this line within Chaupai Sahib daily; Sikh prayer, especially the Ardas, typically widens from oneself to family, community and finally the good of all.

fork.setup: you're the Guru. you've asked for your own protection and your family's peace. who does the prayer turn to next?
options: only the rulers of the land.
my servants and Sikhs: carry them across.
no one else: the prayer is finished.
fork.reveal: sevak sikh hamaare taareeahi: carry my servants and Sikhs across. the circle keeps widening, the way Sikh prayer does.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sevak sikh, servants and disciples, the people the Guru asks God to carry across.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prayer for Sikhs to be kept safe.
what it means: the Guru asking God to ferry his disciples over the world's river, where he himself can't take them.
what a scholar hears: taareeahi is from taarna, to ferry across, the verb behind the Guru Granth Sahib's recurring picture of the world-ocean (bhav sagar) and the boat of the Name.
